chapter_sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: Reproducing organisms create new individuals that look very much like themselves.
The basic event in reproduction is the creation of a DNA copy. DNA (DEOXYRIBO NUCLEIC ACID) is the information source for making proteins.
DNA in the cell nucleus carries information for inheritance of features from parents to the next generation.
If the DNA information changes, different PROTEINS are made, which eventually lead to altered body designs.
DNA copying is accompanied by the creation of additional cellular apparatus; then the cell divides into two cells.
No bio-chemical reaction is absolutely reliable, so DNA copying produces small VARIATIONS each time.
Drastic variations may kill the newborn cell; minor variations make surviving cells similar but subtly different.
This inbuilt tendency for variation during reproduction is the basis for EVOLUTION.

topics.topic_name: DO ORGANISMS CREATE EXACT COPIES OF THEMSELVES?

sections.label: LIST OF SUB-TOPICS:
items: DEFINITION: Reproduction at its most basic level involves making copies of the BLUEPRINTS of body design. Organisms look similar because their body designs (blueprints) are similar, and these blueprints are carried in the form of DNA.

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: Organisms look similar because their body designs are similar; similar body designs need similar blueprints.
The CHROMOSOMES in the nucleus contain information for inheritance of features from parents to offspring in the form of DNA molecules.
A basic event in reproduction is the creation of a DNA copy, done by chemical reactions in the cell.
This creates two copies of DNA in a reproducing cell, which must be separated from each other.
DNA copying is accompanied by creation of an additional cellular apparatus, then the two DNA copies separate, each with its own apparatus; effectively the cell divides into two cells.
The two new cells are similar, but not necessarily absolutely identical, because copying reactions are not perfectly reliable.
Such inaccuracies produce VARIATIONS. Some variations are so drastic that the new DNA copy cannot work and the cell dies.

items.question: What is the basic event in reproduction?
items.answer: The basic event in reproduction is the creation of a DNA copy. Cells use chemical reactions to build copies of their DNA, which is then accompanied by the creation of additional cellular apparatus before the cell divides into two cells.

items.question: Why do organisms of the same species look similar to each other?
items.answer: Organisms look similar because their body designs are similar. Similar body designs require similar blueprints (DNA), so reproduction copies these blueprints and passes them on, making offspring resemble their parents.

items.question: Explain why the two cells formed after reproduction are similar but not absolutely identical.
items.answer: The two new cells are similar because they are formed by copying the same DNA. However, no bio-chemical reaction is absolutely reliable, so the copying process introduces small variations each time. As a result the DNA copies, and hence the cells, are similar but may not be perfectly identical to the original.

items.question: Describe the process of DNA copying during cell division and why an additional cellular apparatus is needed.
items.answer: During reproduction, cells use chemical reactions to make a copy of their DNA, creating two copies in the cell. These copies must be separated from each other. If one copy is simply pushed out, it would have no organised cellular structure to maintain life processes. Therefore, DNA copying is accompanied by the creation of an additional cellular apparatus, and then the two DNA copies separate, each with its own apparatus, so the cell divides into two complete cells.

items.question: How does the DNA in a cell determine the body design of an organism?
items.answer: The chromosomes in the nucleus contain the DNA, which is the information source for making proteins. The proteins built from this information determine the body design. If the DNA information is changed, different proteins are made, which eventually lead to altered body designs. Thus the DNA acts as the blueprint controlling the structure and features of the organism.

items.question: "Reproduction at its most basic level involves making copies of the blueprints of body design." Explain this statement with reference to DNA, proteins and cell division.
items.answer:
Organisms look similar because their body designs are similar, and similar body designs need similar blueprints. These blueprints are stored as DNA in the chromosomes of the cell nucleus. The DNA is the information source for making proteins, and proteins determine body design. Therefore, for a new organism to have the same body design, the cell must first make an accurate copy of its DNA. This is the basic event in reproduction. The cell creates two DNA copies through chemical reactions, builds additional cellular apparatus, and then divides into two cells, each carrying a complete blueprint. Because copying is not perfectly reliable, small variations may arise, which makes offspring similar but not always identical to the parent.

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: Populations of organisms fill well-defined places, or NICHES, in the ecosystem using their ability to reproduce.
Consistency of DNA copying during reproduction maintains body features that allow an organism to use its particular niche.
Reproduction is therefore linked to the stability of populations of species.
NICHES can change due to reasons beyond the control of organisms - temperatures may rise or fall, water levels may vary, or there may be meteorite hits.
If a population is well suited to a niche and the niche is drastically altered, the population could be wiped out.
If some variations are present in a few individuals, there is a chance for some of them to survive the change.
Example: if bacteria living in temperate waters face increased water temperature due to GLOBAL WARMING, most die, but the few heat-resistant variants survive and grow further.
Thus variation is useful for the survival of species over time, even if a particular variation is not always useful to the individual.

items.question: What is a niche?
items.answer: A niche is the well-defined place or role that a population of organisms occupies in the ecosystem, which it fills using its ability to reproduce and its specific body features.

items.question: What is the importance of DNA copying in reproduction?
items.answer: DNA copying ensures that body features needed to use a particular niche are maintained from one generation to the next, giving stability to populations of a species, while also producing small variations.

items.question: Why is variation beneficial to a species but not necessarily to the individual?
items.answer: Variation gives a species a better chance of survival when the environment changes, because at least some variant individuals may be able to survive the new conditions. For an individual, a particular variation may not give any advantage and could even be harmful, but at the population level the presence of variation ensures that the species as a whole can continue.

items.question: How does variation help in the survival of a species when the niche changes? Give an example.
items.answer: When a niche changes drastically, organisms suited only to the old conditions may be wiped out. If variations are present in a few individuals, some of them may survive the altered conditions and reproduce. For example, if bacteria living in temperate waters experience a rise in temperature due to global warming, most of the bacteria die, but a few heat-resistant variants survive and multiply, ensuring the survival of the species.

items.question: Explain how reproduction is linked to the stability of populations of a species.
items.answer: Populations of organisms fill well-defined niches in the ecosystem using their ability to reproduce. The consistency of DNA copying during reproduction maintains the body features that allow an organism to use its particular niche. Because these features are reliably passed on, the population remains suited to its environment, giving stability to the population of that species over generations.

items.question: Discuss the relationship between DNA copying, variation, niches and the survival of species.
items.answer:
During reproduction, DNA is copied so that body features suited to a particular niche are maintained, giving stability to the population. However, DNA copying is not perfectly accurate, so small variations arise among individuals. Niches can change due to factors like temperature change, water level change, or meteorite hits, which are beyond the organisms' control. If a niche is drastically altered and all individuals are identical, the whole population may be wiped out. But if variation exists, a few individuals may be suited to the new conditions and survive. For example, heat-resistant bacterial variants survive global warming while others die. Thus, while consistency of DNA copying maintains the species in stable conditions, variation ensures its survival when conditions change.

topics.topic_name: MODES OF REPRODUCTION USED BY SINGLE ORGANISMS

sections.label: LIST OF SUB-TOPICS:
items: DEFINITION: ASEXUAL REPRODUCTION is the mode of reproduction in which new generations are created from a single individual, without the involvement of two parents or the fusion of germ-cells. The modes used by various organisms depend on their body design.

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: The mode of reproduction used by an organism depends on its body design.
Reproductive processes work differently in unicellular and multicellular organisms.
In multicellular organisms with relatively simple body organisation, simple reproductive methods can still work.
In complex multicellular organisms, specialised cells are organised as tissues and organs placed at definite positions, so simple cell-by-cell division is impractical.
In such organisms, reproduction is the function of a specific cell type that is capable of growing, proliferating and making other cell types under the right circumstances.

All the modes discussed in this topic (fission, fragmentation, regeneration, budding, vegetative propagation, spore formation) allow new generations to be created from a single individual - this is asexual reproduction.

sections.label: ACTIVITY 7.1:
sections.aim: To observe the growth of yeast (budding).
sections.materials: Sugar, water, test tube, yeast granules, cotton plug, microscope, slide, coverslip.
procedure: - Dissolve about 10 gm of sugar in 100 mL of water.
- Take 20 mL of this solution in a test tube and add a pinch of yeast granules to it.
- Put a cotton plug on the mouth of the test tube and keep it in a warm place.
- After 1 or 2 hours, put a small drop of yeast culture from the test tube on a slide and cover it with a coverslip.
- Observe the slide under a microscope.
sections.observation: Yeast cells are seen putting out small buds that separate and grow further.
sections.conclusion: Yeast reproduces asexually by budding, producing small buds that detach and grow into new individuals.

sections.label: ACTIVITY 7.2:
sections.aim: To observe the growth of bread mould (Rhizopus) and compare it with yeast growth.
sections.materials: A slice of bread, a cool moist dark place, magnifying glass.
procedure: - Wet a slice of bread, and keep it in a cool, moist and dark place.
- Observe the surface of the slice with a magnifying glass.
- Record your observations for a week.
sections.observation: Thread-like structures (hyphae) develop on the bread along with tiny blob-on-a-stick structures.
sections.conclusion:
Bread mould (Rhizopus) grows as a mass of thread-like hyphae; the tiny blobs are sporangia containing spores used in reproduction. (Compare and contrast the ways yeast grows in the first case and how mould grows in the second.)

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

items.question: What is asexual reproduction?
items.answer: Asexual reproduction is the mode of reproduction in which new generations are created from a single individual, without the involvement of two parents or fusion of germ-cells.

items.question: On what does the mode of reproduction used by an organism depend?
items.answer: The mode of reproduction used by various organisms depends on their body design - simpler body designs use simpler methods, while complex organisms need more complex modes.

items.question: Why can complex multicellular organisms not reproduce by simple cell-by-cell division?
items.answer: In complex multicellular organisms, specialised cells are organised as tissues, and tissues are organised into organs placed at definite positions in the body. In such a carefully organised situation, cell-by-cell division would be impractical, so these organisms need more complex modes of reproduction carried out by a specific cell type.

items.question: Name any four modes of asexual reproduction and one organism that uses each.
items.answer: (i) Fission - Amoeba; (ii) Fragmentation - Spirogyra; (iii) Regeneration - Hydra or Planaria; (iv) Budding - Hydra or yeast. (Spore formation - Rhizopus; Vegetative propagation - Bryophyllum are also acceptable examples.)

items.question: How is reproduction achieved in complex multicellular organisms from a single cell type?
items.answer: A basic strategy in multicellular organisms is that different cell types perform different specialised functions, and reproduction too is the function of a specific cell type. There must be a single cell type in the organism that is capable of growing, proliferating and making other cell types under the right circumstances. From this cell type, new individuals can develop.

items.question: Describe how reproductive strategies differ between simple and complex multicellular organisms.
items.answer:
In multicellular organisms with relatively simple body organisation, simple reproductive methods can still work; for example, Spirogyra simply breaks up into smaller fragments upon maturation, and each fragment grows into a new individual. However, this is not true for all multicellular organisms. Many of them are not a random collection of cells; specialised cells are organised as tissues, and tissues into organs placed at definite positions. In such a carefully organised body, cell-by-cell division would be impractical. Therefore complex multicellular organisms use more complex ways of reproduction. A basic strategy is that different cell types perform specialised functions, and reproduction becomes the function of a specific cell type that can grow, proliferate and make other cell types under the right circumstances.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: For unicellular organisms, cell division or fission leads to the creation of new individuals.
Many bacteria and protozoa simply split into two equal halves during cell division - this is BINARY FISSION.
In organisms such as Amoeba, the splitting of the two cells during division can take place in any plane.

Some unicellular organisms show more organisation of their bodies, such as Leishmania (which cause kala-azar), which have a whip-like structure at one end of the cell; in such organisms binary fission occurs in a definite orientation in relation to these structures.
The malarial parasite Plasmodium divides into many daughter cells simultaneously by MULTIPLE FISSION.

items.question: What is binary fission?
items.answer: Binary fission is a mode of asexual reproduction in which a unicellular organism simply splits into two equal halves during cell division, as seen in many bacteria and protozoa.

items.question: How does binary fission differ from multiple fission?
items.answer: In binary fission a cell splits into two daughter cells, whereas in multiple fission a single cell divides into many daughter cells simultaneously, as in Plasmodium.

items.question: Describe binary fission in Amoeba.
items.answer: In Amoeba, a unicellular organism, reproduction takes place by binary fission. The cell divides into two equal halves, and this splitting can take place in any plane. Each daughter cell then grows into a new Amoeba.

items.question: How does binary fission in Leishmania differ from that in Amoeba?
items.answer: In Amoeba, the splitting of the cell during binary fission can take place in any plane because the body has no particular organisation. In Leishmania, the cell has more organisation with a whip-like structure at one end; therefore binary fission occurs in a definite orientation in relation to this whip-like structure, not in any random plane.

items.question: Explain multiple fission with an example.
items.answer: Multiple fission is a mode of asexual reproduction in which a single cell divides into many daughter cells simultaneously. The malarial parasite Plasmodium reproduces by multiple fission, producing many daughter cells at the same time from one parent cell. This allows it to increase its numbers rapidly.

items.question: Compare binary fission and multiple fission, giving examples and the role of body organisation.
items.answer:
Both binary and multiple fission are modes of asexual reproduction in unicellular organisms based on cell division. In binary fission, the cell splits into two equal daughter cells; many bacteria and protozoa, including Amoeba, reproduce this way. In Amoeba the split can occur in any plane, but in more organised organisms like Leishmania, which have a whip-like structure at one end, fission occurs in a definite orientation relative to that structure. In multiple fission, a single cell divides into many daughter cells simultaneously; the malarial parasite Plasmodium reproduces this way. Thus the degree of body organisation influences the plane and pattern of fission, while the number of daughter cells produced distinguishes binary from multiple fission.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Spirogyra, for example, simply breaks up into smaller pieces upon maturation.
These pieces or fragments grow into new individuals.
Fragmentation is not possible for all multicellular organisms, because in complex organisms cells are organised as specialised tissues and organs, making cell-by-cell division impractical.

items.question: What is fragmentation?
items.answer: Fragmentation is a mode of asexual reproduction in which a simple multicellular organism breaks up into smaller pieces on maturation, and each piece grows into a new individual.

items.question: Explain fragmentation with the example of Spirogyra.
items.answer: Spirogyra is a simple multicellular organism. On maturation, it simply breaks up into smaller pieces or fragments. Each of these fragments then grows into a new Spirogyra individual, so fragmentation acts as its method of asexual reproduction.

items.question: Why can fragmentation work in Spirogyra but not in complex multicellular organisms?
items.answer:
Spirogyra has a relatively simple body organisation, so when it breaks into pieces, each piece can grow into a new organism. In complex multicellular organisms, however, specialised cells are organised into tissues and organs placed at definite positions. Breaking such an organism into fragments would not produce a properly organised body, so cell-by-cell division or fragmentation is impractical and they use more complex modes of reproduction.

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: Many fully differentiated organisms have the ability to give rise to new individuals from their body parts.
If the individual is somehow cut or broken up into many pieces, many of these pieces grow into separate individuals.
Examples are simple animals like Hydra and Planaria, which can be cut into any number of pieces, and each piece grows into a complete organism.
Regeneration is carried out by SPECIALISED CELLS. These cells proliferate and make large numbers of cells.
From this mass of cells, different cells undergo changes to become various cell types and tissues.
These changes take place in an organised sequence referred to as DEVELOPMENT.
However, regeneration is NOT the same as reproduction, since most organisms would not normally depend on being cut up to be able to reproduce.

items.question: What is regeneration?
items.answer: Regeneration is the ability of fully differentiated organisms to give rise to new individuals from their body parts; if cut into pieces, many pieces grow into separate complete individuals.

items.question: Name two organisms that show regeneration.
items.answer: Simple animals like Hydra and Planaria show regeneration; they can be cut into pieces and each piece grows into a complete organism.

items.question: How is regeneration carried out in organisms like Planaria?
items.answer: Regeneration is carried out by specialised cells. These cells proliferate and make large numbers of cells. From this mass of cells, different cells undergo changes to become various cell types and tissues, in an organised sequence called development, finally forming a complete organism.

items.question: Why is regeneration not considered the same as reproduction?
items.answer: Although regeneration produces new individuals from body parts, it is not considered true reproduction because most organisms would not normally depend on being cut up into pieces to reproduce. Regeneration happens only when the body is accidentally cut or broken, whereas reproduction is a regular, normal process. Therefore regeneration is an ability of certain organisms, not their usual mode of producing offspring.

items.question: Explain the role of specialised cells and development in regeneration.
items.answer: Regeneration is carried out by specialised cells. When the organism is cut, these cells proliferate to make large numbers of cells. From this mass of cells, different cells undergo changes to become various cell types and tissues. These changes occur in an organised sequence referred to as development, which ensures that the new body parts and the whole organism are properly formed.

items.question: Describe the process of regeneration in simple animals and explain why it differs from reproduction.
items.answer:
Many fully differentiated simple animals, such as Hydra and Planaria, have the ability to give rise to new individuals from their body parts. If such an organism is cut or broken into many pieces, many of these pieces grow into separate individuals. This is carried out by specialised cells that proliferate to form a large mass of cells. From this mass, different cells undergo organised changes to become various cell types and tissues, a sequence called development, finally producing complete organisms. However, regeneration is not the same as reproduction, because most organisms would not normally depend on being cut up to reproduce. Reproduction is the regular method by which a species multiplies, while regeneration is a special ability that operates only when the body is broken.

points: Organisms such as Hydra use regenerative cells for reproduction in the process of budding.
In Hydra, a bud develops as an outgrowth due to repeated cell division at one specific site.
These buds develop into tiny individuals.
When fully mature, the buds detach from the parent body and become new independent individuals.
Yeast also reproduces by budding (as seen in Activity 7.1), putting out small buds that separate and grow further.

items.question: What is budding?
items.answer: Budding is a mode of asexual reproduction in which a bud develops as an outgrowth on the parent body by repeated cell division at one site, and later detaches to form a new individual.

items.question: Name two organisms that reproduce by budding.
items.answer: Hydra and yeast reproduce by budding; both produce buds that grow and then separate to become new individuals.

items.question: Describe budding in Hydra.
items.answer: In Hydra, a bud develops as an outgrowth due to repeated cell division at one specific site, using regenerative cells. This bud develops into a tiny individual, and when fully mature, it detaches from the parent body and becomes a new independent individual.

items.question: How does budding in Hydra take place using regenerative cells?
items.answer: Hydra uses regenerative cells for reproduction by budding. At one specific site on the body, these cells undergo repeated cell division, forming a bud that grows out from the parent. The bud develops into a tiny but complete individual. Once it is fully mature, the bud detaches from the parent and lives as a separate independent organism.

items.question: How is budding in yeast similar to and different from budding in Hydra?
items.answer: In both yeast and Hydra, budding involves the formation of a small bud on the parent that grows and then separates to form a new individual. The similarity is that both produce buds by cell division and the buds detach to become independent. The difference is that yeast is a unicellular organism producing small buds from a single cell, while Hydra is a simple multicellular animal that produces a multicellular bud using regenerative cells.

items.question: Explain the process of budding in detail with reference to Hydra, and state how it is an example of asexual reproduction.
items.answer:
Budding is a mode of asexual reproduction seen in organisms such as Hydra, which use regenerative cells for reproduction. The process begins at one specific site on the parent body, where repeated cell division produces a small outgrowth called a bud. This bud grows and develops into a tiny individual complete with its own body parts. When the bud is fully mature, it detaches from the parent body and becomes a new independent individual. Because a single parent produces the offspring without the involvement of a second parent or fusion of germ-cells, budding is a form of asexual reproduction. Yeast also reproduces in a similar way, putting out small buds that separate and grow further.

items.question: What is spore formation?
items.answer: Spore formation is a mode of asexual reproduction in which sporangia produce tiny spores covered by thick walls, which develop into new individuals when they reach a suitable moist surface.

items.question: What are sporangia?

items.answer: An organism reproducing through spores produces large numbers of spores covered by thick protective walls. This protection allows the spores to survive dry or harsh conditions and ensures successful reproduction when a suitable surface is available.

items.question: Explain spore formation as a mode of asexual reproduction using Rhizopus as an example.

Spore formation is a mode of asexual reproduction seen in simple multicellular organisms such as the bread mould Rhizopus. On the bread, Rhizopus develops thread-like structures called hyphae; however, these hyphae are not reproductive parts. The reproductive structures are the tiny blob-on-a-stick structures called sporangia. Each sporangium contains many cells called spores. These spores are covered by thick protective walls, which guard them until they come into contact with another moist surface. Once on a suitable moist surface, each spore can germinate and develop into a new Rhizopus individual. In this way, a single organism produces many new individuals asexually, and the thick-walled spores help the species survive unfavourable conditions and spread to new places.

items: 7.3.1 Why the Sexual Mode of Reproduction?

DEFINITION: SEXUAL REPRODUCTION is the mode of reproduction that depends on the involvement of two individuals (parents) before a new generation can be created, by combining DNA from two different individuals through the fusion of germ-cells (gametes).

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: We are familiar with modes of reproduction that depend on the involvement of two individuals before a new generation can be created.
Bulls alone cannot produce new calves, nor can hens alone produce new chicks; both sexes, males and females, are needed.
Sexual reproduction incorporates a process of combining DNA from two different individuals during reproduction.
This combining of variations from two or more individuals creates new combinations of variants, and each combination is novel.
Sexual reproduction therefore allows for greater variation to be generated compared to asexual reproduction.

items.question: What is sexual reproduction?
items.answer: Sexual reproduction is the mode of reproduction that depends on the involvement of two individuals and combines DNA from two different individuals through the fusion of germ-cells before a new generation is created.

items.question: Why can a bull or a hen not produce offspring alone?
items.answer: A bull alone cannot produce new calves and a hen alone cannot produce new chicks because in sexual reproduction both sexes, males and females, are needed to create a new individual.

items.question: How does sexual reproduction help create new combinations of variants?
items.answer: Sexual reproduction combines DNA from two different individuals. Since each individual already has different patterns of accumulated variations, combining variations from two individuals creates new combinations of variants. Each such combination is novel because it involves two different individuals, which speeds up the generation of variation.

items.question: Why does sexual reproduction allow for greater variation than asexual reproduction?
items.answer: In asexual reproduction, variation arises only from slow, small errors in DNA copying. In sexual reproduction, DNA from two different individuals is combined. Each individual carries its own accumulated variations, so combining them produces new combinations of variants that are novel. This combination of variations from two individuals generates much greater variation than the slow process of copying errors in asexual reproduction.

items.question: Explain how each new variation is built on previous variations in sexual reproduction.
items.answer: Each new variation is made in a DNA copy that already has variations accumulated from previous generations. Thus two different individuals in a population have quite different patterns of accumulated variations. Since these variations are present in living individuals, they do not have really bad effects. Combining variations from two such individuals during sexual reproduction creates new, novel combinations of variants, speeding up the generation of useful variation.

items.question: Discuss the significance of sexual reproduction in generating variation.
items.answer:
Sexual reproduction depends on combining DNA from two different individuals. DNA copying mechanisms in cells are precise enough that the generation of variation by errors alone is a slow process. To speed this up, each new variation is made in a DNA copy that already carries variations accumulated from previous generations. Two different individuals in a population therefore have quite different patterns of accumulated variations, and since these variations exist in living individuals, they do not have really harmful effects. By combining variations from two or more individuals, sexual reproduction creates new combinations of variants, each of which is novel because it involves two different individuals. This is why sexual modes of reproduction allow for much greater variation to be generated than asexual reproduction, which is important for the survival and evolution of species.

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: The creation of two new cells from one involves copying of the DNA as well as the cellular apparatus.
DNA copying mechanisms are not absolutely accurate, and the resultant errors are a source of VARIATIONS in populations of organisms.
Variations are useful for ensuring the survival of the species, though an individual may not be protected by them.
DNA copying is precise enough that generation of variation by errors alone is a fairly slow process.
Each new variation is made in a DNA copy that already has variations accumulated from previous generations, so two different individuals have quite different patterns of accumulated variations.
Since these variations are present in living individuals, they do not have really bad effects; combining variations from two or more individuals creates novel combinations.
PROBLEM: If each new generation simply combined DNA copies from two pre-existing individuals, each generation would have twice the amount of DNA, messing up the control of the cellular apparatus.

SOLUTION: Many multicellular organisms have special lineages of cells in specialised organs in which only HALF the number of chromosomes and half the amount of DNA are present compared to non-reproductive body cells. This is achieved by a process of cell division called MEIOSIS.
When these germ-cells from two individuals combine during sexual reproduction, the normal chromosome number and DNA content of the new generation is re-established.
If the ZYGOTE is to grow and develop into an organism with highly specialised tissues and organs, it must have sufficient stores of energy for doing this.
In very simple organisms, the two germ-cells may not be very different, or may even be similar.

As body designs become complex, the germ-cells also specialise: one germ-cell is large and contains the food-stores (the FEMALE GAMETE), while the other is smaller and likely to be motile (the MALE GAMETE).

items.question: What is meiosis?
items.answer: Meiosis is a process of cell division that produces germ-cells (gametes) having only half the number of chromosomes and half the amount of DNA compared to the non-reproductive body cells.

items.question: Distinguish between the male gamete and the female gamete.
items.answer: The male gamete is smaller and likely to be motile, while the female gamete is large and contains the food-stores needed by the developing organism.

items.question: Why do germ-cells have half the number of chromosomes?
items.answer: If germ-cells had the full number of chromosomes, combining DNA from two individuals would double the DNA in each generation, disturbing the control of the cellular apparatus. To prevent this, germ-cells are formed by meiosis with half the chromosomes and half the DNA. When two germ-cells combine, the normal chromosome number is re-established in the new individual.

items.question: How is the problem of doubling DNA in each generation solved in sexual reproduction?
items.answer: If each new generation simply combined DNA copies from two individuals, each generation would have twice the amount of DNA, which would mess up the control of the cellular apparatus. The problem is solved by having special lineages of cells in specialised organs that contain only half the number of chromosomes and half the amount of DNA, formed by a cell division called meiosis. When these germ-cells from two individuals combine during sexual reproduction, the original chromosome number and DNA content of the new generation are re-established.

items.question: Why do the two germ-cells become different from each other as body designs become complex?
items.answer: As body designs become complex, the zygote needs to grow and develop into an organism with highly specialised tissues and organs, which requires sufficient stores of energy. To meet this need, the germ-cells specialise: one germ-cell becomes large and stores food (the female gamete) to nourish the developing organism, while the other becomes small and motile (the male gamete) so that it can move towards the female germ-cell. In very simple organisms, where this is not needed, the two germ-cells may be similar.

items.question: Explain why the sexual mode of reproduction is advantageous, with reference to variation, meiosis and germ-cells.
items.answer:
The creation of new cells involves DNA copying, which is precise but not absolutely accurate, so it produces variations useful for species survival; however, variation by copying errors alone is slow. Sexual reproduction speeds this up by combining DNA from two different individuals, each of which already carries different accumulated variations, creating novel combinations of variants. But combining DNA from two individuals would double the DNA each generation. This is solved by meiosis, a cell division that produces germ-cells with half the chromosome number and half the DNA. When two germ-cells fuse, the normal chromosome number is restored. Furthermore, as body designs become complex, the germ-cells specialise into a large food-storing female gamete and a small motile male gamete, so that the zygote has the energy stores needed to develop into a complex organism. Thus the sexual mode provides greater variation while keeping the DNA content stable and supporting development.

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: The reproductive parts of angiosperms are located in the FLOWER.
The different parts of a flower are SEPALS, PETALS, STAMENS and PISTIL. Stamens and pistil are the reproductive parts containing the germ-cells.
A flower may be UNISEXUAL (papaya, watermelon) when it contains either stamens or pistil, or BISEXUAL (Hibiscus, mustard) when it contains both stamens and pistil.
STAMEN is the male reproductive part; it produces yellowish pollen grains.

PISTIL is present in the centre of the flower and is the female reproductive part, made of three parts: the swollen bottom part is the OVARY, the middle elongated part is the STYLE, and the terminal part (which may be sticky) is the STIGMA.
The ovary contains OVULES, and each ovule has an egg cell.
The male germ-cell produced by the pollen grain fuses with the female gamete present in the ovule; this fusion (FERTILISATION) gives the ZYGOTE, which grows into a new plant.

POLLINATION is the transfer of pollen from the stamen (anther) to the stigma. If transfer occurs in the same flower, it is SELF-POLLINATION; if from one flower to another, it is CROSS-POLLINATION, achieved by agents like wind, water or animals.
After pollination, a tube grows out of the pollen grain and travels through the style to reach the ovary and the female germ-cells.
After fertilisation, the zygote divides several times to form an EMBRYO within the ovule. The ovule develops a tough coat and gradually becomes a SEED.
The ovary grows rapidly and ripens to form a FRUIT, while the petals, sepals, stamens, style and stigma may shrivel and fall off.
The seed contains the future plant or embryo, which develops into a seedling under appropriate conditions - this process is known as GERMINATION.

items.question: Name the parts of a pistil.
items.answer: The pistil is made of three parts: the swollen bottom part is the ovary, the middle elongated part is the style, and the terminal part is the stigma.

items.question: What is the difference between a unisexual and a bisexual flower?
items.answer: A unisexual flower contains either stamens or pistil (for example, papaya, watermelon), while a bisexual flower contains both stamens and pistil (for example, Hibiscus, mustard).

items.question: How is the process of pollination different from fertilisation?
items.answer: Pollination is the transfer of pollen grains from the anther (stamen) to the stigma, carried out by agents like wind, water or animals. Fertilisation is the fusion of the male germ-cell from the pollen grain with the female gamete present in the ovule, which forms the zygote. Thus pollination occurs first and brings the germ-cells closer, while fertilisation is the actual fusion that follows.

items.question: Describe what happens after pollen lands on a suitable stigma.
items.answer: After the pollen lands on a suitable stigma, a tube grows out of the pollen grain and travels through the style to reach the ovary, where the female germ-cells are present. The male germ-cell produced by the pollen grain then fuses with the female gamete in the ovule. This fusion, called fertilisation, produces the zygote, which is capable of growing into a new plant.

items.question: Describe the changes that take place in a flower after fertilisation.
items.answer: After fertilisation, the zygote divides several times to form an embryo within the ovule. The ovule develops a tough coat and is gradually converted into a seed. The ovary grows rapidly and ripens to form a fruit. Meanwhile, the petals, sepals, stamens, style and stigma may shrivel and fall off. The seed contains the future plant (embryo), which develops into a seedling under appropriate conditions through germination.

items.question: With the help of the parts of a flower, explain sexual reproduction in flowering plants from pollination to seed formation.
items.answer:
The reproductive parts of a flowering plant are the stamen (male) and the pistil (female). The stamen produces pollen grains, and the pistil consists of the stigma, style and ovary, with the ovary containing ovules that have egg cells. Reproduction begins with pollination, the transfer of pollen from the anther to the stigma, which may be self-pollination (same flower) or cross-pollination (different flowers) by agents like wind, water or animals. After pollen lands on a suitable stigma, a pollen tube grows through the style to reach the ovary. The male germ-cell then fuses with the female gamete in the ovule - this fertilisation forms the zygote. The zygote divides repeatedly to form an embryo inside the ovule, which develops a tough coat to become a seed, while the ovary ripens into a fruit and the other floral parts shrivel. The seed contains the embryo, which germinates into a new seedling under suitable conditions.

sections.label: KEY POINTS (OVERVIEW):
points: Humans use a sexual mode of reproduction, in which germ-cells from two individuals join together.
This joining happens by two individuals joining their bodies together for internal transfer of germ-cells for fusion, as in many animals.
For mating, the state of sexual maturity of individuals must be identifiable by other individuals.
Our bodies change as we grow older; height increases, milk teeth are lost and new teeth appear.

In early teenage years, a new set of changes occurs that cannot be explained simply by body enlargement; the appearance of the body changes, proportions change, new features appear and new sensations develop.
The period during adolescence when reproductive tissues begin to mature is called PUBERTY.

Changes common to both boys and girls: thick hair grows in new parts such as armpits and the genital area (which can also become darker), thinner hair appears on legs, arms and face, the skin frequently becomes oily and pimples may develop, and we become conscious of our own bodies and those of others.
Changes in girls: breast size begins to increase with darkening of the skin of the nipples, and girls begin to menstruate.
Changes in boys: thick hair growth on the face, voices begin to crack, and the penis occasionally begins to become enlarged and erect.
These changes take place slowly over months and years, not all at the same time, and at different ages in different people.
During puberty, as general body growth slows down, the reproductive tissues begin to mature.
The creation of germ-cells to participate in sexual reproduction is a specialised function; humans develop special tissues for this purpose.

DEFINITION: The MALE REPRODUCTIVE SYSTEM consists of the parts that produce the germ-cells (sperms) and the parts that deliver these germ-cells to the site of fertilisation.

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: The male reproductive system consists of portions that produce the germ-cells and other portions that deliver the germ-cells to the site of fertilisation.
The formation of germ-cells or SPERMS takes place in the TESTES.
The testes are located outside the abdominal cavity in the SCROTUM, because sperm formation requires a lower temperature than the normal body temperature.
The testes secrete the hormone TESTOSTERONE; besides regulating the formation of sperms, testosterone brings about changes in appearance seen in boys at the time of puberty.
The sperms formed are delivered through the VAS DEFERENS, which unites with a tube coming from the urinary bladder.
The URETHRA thus forms a common passage for both the sperms and urine.
Along the path of the vas deferens, glands like the PROSTATE and the SEMINAL VESICLES add their secretions, so the sperms are now in a fluid which makes their transport easier and provides nutrition.
The sperms are tiny bodies that consist mainly of genetic material and a long tail that helps them move towards the female germ-cell.

DEFINITION: The FEMALE REPRODUCTIVE SYSTEM produces the female germ-cells (eggs) in the ovaries and provides the site where fertilisation and the development of the baby take place.

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: The female germ-cells or EGGS are made in the OVARIES.
The ovaries are also responsible for the production of some hormones.
When a girl is born, the ovaries already contain thousands of immature eggs; on reaching puberty, some of these start maturing.
One egg is produced every month by one of the ovaries.
The egg is carried from the ovary to the womb through a thin OVIDUCT or FALLOPIAN TUBE.
The two oviducts unite into an elastic bag-like structure known as the UTERUS.
The uterus opens into the VAGINA through the CERVIX.
The sperms enter through the vaginal passage during sexual intercourse; they travel upwards and reach the oviduct, where they may encounter the egg.
The fertilised egg, the ZYGOTE, starts dividing and forms a ball of cells or EMBRYO.
The embryo is implanted in the lining of the uterus, where it continues to grow and develop organs to become a FOETUS.
The lining of the uterus thickens and is richly supplied with blood to nourish the growing embryo.
The embryo gets nutrition from the mother's blood with the help of a special tissue called the PLACENTA, a disc embedded in the uterine wall.

The placenta contains VILLI on the embryo's side; on the mother's side are blood spaces which surround the villi, providing a large surface area for glucose and oxygen to pass from the mother to the embryo.
Waste substances produced by the developing embryo are removed by transferring them into the mother's blood through the placenta.
The development of the child inside the mother's body takes approximately NINE MONTHS.
The child is born as a result of rhythmic contractions of the muscles in the uterus.

DEFINITION: MENSTRUATION is the process in which the thick, blood-rich lining of the uterus breaks down and is shed through the vagina when the released egg is not fertilised; this cycle occurs roughly every month.

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: If the egg is not fertilised, it lives for about one day.
Since the ovary releases one egg every month, the uterus also prepares itself every month to receive a fertilised egg, so its lining becomes thick and spongy.
This thick lining would be required for nourishing the embryo if fertilisation had taken place.
If fertilisation does not occur, this lining is not needed any longer.
So the lining slowly breaks and comes out through the vagina as blood and mucous.
This cycle takes place roughly every month and is known as MENSTRUATION; it usually lasts for about two to eight days.

DEFINITION: REPRODUCTIVE HEALTH refers to the state of physical and mental readiness for sexual maturation, sexual acts, and having and raising children, along with the prevention of sexually transmitted diseases and the regulation of pregnancy.

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: Sexual maturation is gradual and takes place while general body growth is still going on, so some degree of sexual maturation does not necessarily mean the body or mind is ready for sexual acts or for having and bringing up children.

People are under many kinds of pressures about these issues - from friends, families to get married and have children, and from government agencies to avoid having children - which makes choices difficult.
Diseases can be transmitted during the sexual act because it is a very intimate connection of bodies; these are sexually transmitted diseases.
Bacterial infections such as GONORRHOEA and SYPHILIS, and viral infections such as WARTS and HIV-AIDS can be sexually transmitted.
Using a covering called a CONDOM for the penis during sex helps to prevent the transmission of many of these infections to some extent.

The sexual act always has the potential to lead to pregnancy, which makes major demands on the body and mind of the woman; if she is not ready, her health is adversely affected. So many CONTRACEPTIVE methods have been devised to avoid pregnancy.
Contraceptive methods fall into several categories:
(i) Mechanical barrier - creating a barrier (such as a condom) so that sperm does not reach the egg.
(ii) Hormonal/oral pills - changing the hormonal balance of the body so that eggs are not released; these are commonly taken orally as pills but can cause side-effects.
(iii) Devices in the uterus - the loop or the copper-T are placed in the uterus to prevent pregnancy; they can cause side effects due to irritation of the uterus.

(iv) Surgical methods - if the vas deferens in the male is blocked, sperm transfer is prevented; if the fallopian tube in the female is blocked, the egg cannot reach the uterus; in both cases fertilisation will not take place.
Surgical methods are safe in the long run but surgery itself can cause infections and other problems if not performed properly.
Surgery can also be used for removal of unwanted pregnancies, but this may be misused for illegal sex-selective abortion of female foetuses.

For a healthy society, the female-male sex ratio must be maintained; reckless female foeticides are causing the child sex ratio to decline at an alarming rate, although prenatal sex determination has been prohibited by law.

Reproduction increases populations; rates of birth and death determine the size of a population. The size of the human population is a cause of concern because an expanding population makes it harder to improve everybody's standard of living, though inequality in society may be a more important reason for poor living standards.

items.question: What is puberty?
items.answer: Puberty is the period during adolescence when the reproductive tissues begin to mature and the body shows signs of sexual maturation, as general body growth slows down.

items.question: Where are sperms produced and why are the testes located in the scrotum?
items.answer: Sperms are produced in the testes. The testes are located outside the abdominal cavity in the scrotum because sperm formation requires a temperature lower than the normal body temperature.

items.question: What are the changes seen in girls at the time of puberty?
items.answer: At puberty in girls, the breast size begins to increase with darkening of the skin of the nipples, and girls begin to menstruate. Along with these, common changes also occur such as growth of thick hair in the armpits and genital area and the skin becoming oily.

items.question: How does the embryo get nourishment inside the mother's body?
items.answer: The embryo gets nutrition from the mother's blood with the help of a special tissue called the placenta, which is a disc embedded in the uterine wall. The placenta contains villi on the embryo's side, and on the mother's side are blood spaces surrounding the villi. This provides a large surface area for glucose and oxygen to pass from the mother to the embryo, while waste substances generated by the embryo are removed into the mother's blood through the placenta.

items.question: Why does menstruation occur?
items.answer: Menstruation occurs when the egg released by the ovary is not fertilised. The ovary releases one egg every month, and in preparation the uterus develops a thick and spongy lining richly supplied with blood to nourish a possible embryo. If fertilisation does not take place, this lining is not needed, so it slowly breaks down and is shed through the vagina as blood and mucous. This cycle repeats roughly every month and usually lasts about two to eight days.

items.question: Trace the path of the egg and describe what happens after fertilisation in human beings.
items.answer:
One egg is produced every month by one of the ovaries. The egg is carried from the ovary to the womb through a thin oviduct or fallopian tube. The two oviducts unite into an elastic bag-like structure called the uterus, which opens into the vagina through the cervix. During sexual intercourse, sperms enter through the vaginal passage, travel upwards and reach the oviduct, where they may encounter the egg. If a sperm fertilises the egg, the fertilised egg (zygote) starts dividing to form a ball of cells or embryo. This embryo is implanted in the thickened lining of the uterus, where it grows and develops organs to become a foetus, getting nutrition from the mother's blood through the placenta. The development takes about nine months, after which the child is born as a result of rhythmic contractions of the muscles in the uterus.

sections.label: WHAT YOU HAVE LEARNT (CHAPTER SUMMARY)
sections.text:
- Reproduction, unlike other life processes, is not essential to maintain the life of an individual organism.
- Reproduction involves creation of a DNA copy and additional cellular apparatus by the cell involved in the process.
- Various organisms use different modes of reproduction depending on their body design.
- In fission, many bacteria and protozoa simply divide into two or more daughter cells.
- Organisms such as Hydra can regenerate if they are broken into pieces. They can also give out buds which mature into new individuals.
- Roots, stems and leaves of some plants develop into new plants through vegetative propagation.
- These are examples of asexual reproduction where new generations are created from a single individual.
- Sexual reproduction involves two individuals for the creation of a new individual.
- DNA copying mechanisms create variations which are useful for ensuring the survival of the species. Modes of sexual reproduction allow for greater variation to be generated.
- Reproduction in flowering plants involves transfer of pollen grains from the anther to the stigma, which is referred to as pollination. This is followed by fertilisation.
- Changes in the body at puberty, such as increase in breast size in girls and new facial hair growth in boys, are signs of sexual maturation.
- The male reproductive system in human beings consists of testes which produce sperms, vas deferens, seminal vesicles, prostate gland, urethra and penis.
- The female reproductive system in human beings consists of ovaries, fallopian tubes, uterus and vagina.
- Sexual reproduction in human beings involves the introduction of sperm in the vagina of the female. Fertilisation occurs in the fallopian tube.
- Contraception to avoid pregnancy can be achieved by the use of condoms, oral pills, copper-T and other methods.

sections.label: EXERCISE 7.1:
sections.raw:
Q: Asexual reproduction takes place through budding in
(a) Amoeba.  (b) Yeast.  (c) Plasmodium.  (d) Leishmania.
A: (b) Yeast. Yeast reproduces by budding, putting out small buds that separate and grow into new individuals.

sections.label: EXERCISE 7.2:
sections.raw:
Q: Which of the following is not a part of the female reproductive system in human beings?
(a) Ovary  (b) Uterus  (c) Vas deferens  (d) Fallopian tube
A: (c) Vas deferens. The vas deferens is part of the MALE reproductive system; ovary, uterus and fallopian tube belong to the female reproductive system.

sections.label: EXERCISE 7.3:
sections.raw:
Q: The anther contains
(a) sepals.  (b) ovules.  (c) pistil.  (d) pollen grains.
A: (d) pollen grains. The anther is part of the stamen (male part) and produces pollen grains.

sections.label: EXERCISE 7.4:
sections.raw:
Q: What are the advantages of sexual reproduction over asexual reproduction?
A: In sexual reproduction, DNA from two different individuals is combined, creating new combinations of variants. This generates much greater variation than the slow process of copying errors in asexual reproduction. Greater variation gives the species a better chance of survival when the environment changes and is important for evolution.

sections.label: EXERCISE 7.5:
sections.raw:
Q: What are the functions performed by the testis in human beings?
A: The testis performs two main functions: (i) it produces the male germ-cells, the sperms, and (ii) it secretes the hormone testosterone, which regulates the formation of sperms and brings about the changes in appearance seen in boys at the time of puberty.

sections.label: EXERCISE 7.6:
sections.raw:
Q: Why does menstruation occur?
A: The ovary releases one egg every month, and the uterus prepares a thick, blood-rich lining to receive a possible fertilised egg. If the egg is not fertilised, this lining is not needed and slowly breaks down, coming out through the vagina as blood and mucous. This monthly shedding is called menstruation and usually lasts about two to eight days.

sections.label: EXERCISE 7.8:
sections.raw:
Q: What are the different methods of contraception?
A: The different methods of contraception are: (i) mechanical barrier methods such as the condom, which prevent sperm from reaching the egg; (ii) hormonal methods such as oral pills that change the hormonal balance so that eggs are not released; (iii) intra-uterine devices such as the loop or copper-T placed in the uterus; and (iv) surgical methods, in which the vas deferens in the male or the fallopian tube in the female is blocked so that fertilisation cannot take place.

sections.label: EXERCISE 7.9:
sections.raw:
Q: How are the modes for reproduction different in unicellular and multicellular organisms?
A: Unicellular organisms reproduce by simple methods based on cell division, such as fission (binary fission in Amoeba, multiple fission in Plasmodium). Multicellular organisms, especially complex ones, have specialised cells organised into tissues and organs, so cell-by-cell division is impractical. They use more complex modes such as regeneration, budding, vegetative propagation, spore formation, or sexual reproduction involving specialised germ-cells.

sections.label: EXERCISE 7.10:
sections.raw:
Q: How does reproduction help in providing stability to populations of species?
A: Populations fill well-defined niches in the ecosystem using their ability to reproduce. The consistency of DNA copying during reproduction maintains the body features that allow organisms to use their niche, so the population stays well suited to its environment. This passing on of suitable features from generation to generation gives stability to the population of a species.

sections.label: EXERCISE 7.11:
sections.raw:
Q: What could be the reasons for adopting contraceptive methods?
A: Contraceptive methods are adopted to (i) avoid unwanted pregnancy, since the sexual act always has the potential to lead to pregnancy and pregnancy makes major demands on the body and mind of the woman; (ii) prevent the transmission of sexually transmitted diseases (for example, condoms help prevent many infections); and (iii) help control the size of the human population, since an expanding population makes it harder to improve everybody's standard of living.
